comments.text:
I don't think it is a geological problem. Yes, people settled first were it was easiest to start a civilization but after that it is governments and economics that force where people live.
What you explain in this video isn't only happening in Canada. It happens world wide. About a decade ago, it was projected that 80% of the population would live in cities by 2050. Well, we already reached that projection. Where in the past (few decades ago) small rural towns 2 - 3 hours drive from a major city, flourished. They are now or becoming ghost towns.
Even though the technology is so much more advanced nowadays, that living in remote areas could be a piece of mind. It is not that difficult to build on solid rock (isn't Manhattan build on solid rock?)
It all depends on politics and where/how to get the most GDP.
Grand Prairie (northwest of Edmonton) and Fort McMurray (northeast of Edmonton) are both 4.5 to 5 hour (in the boonies) from Edmonton, and both flourishing (for now) with a population of 60,000+. The reason? Oil and gas production. Oil and gas is for 25+% Alberta's GDP
Canada is not full and it is totally feasible to live on rock or further north in the boonies. But it's not economical. It is more economical (and for some cooler) to live in sky scrapers.
When I moved 3 decades ago from the Netherlands to Canada most of the urban expansion was  single household free standing homes. After a recession and covid, nowadays, single household houses are not profitable any more for developers. With the result that developers building multi household structures. And still, for the occupants it cost more than a free standing home 3 decades ago (even with the inflation conversion)

Maybe this is a nice fact: If Canada had the population density of the Netherlands. It would have a population of over 4 billion. Or half the global population.

comments.author: @jondevaney6860
comments.text:
Geoff, the central message of your video is the term "ecumene." I learned this in high school geography class (in Toronto, back in the 1970s) - a teacher explained how the population ecumene (settled area) of Canada was strung out along the southern boundary, forming what is in effect a long narrow country (a bit similar to Chile, in a vague way).

A key point of Canadian geography theory is nodes versus "hinterlands." Nodes are the cities and towns, and they are surrounded, at large scales, by hinterlands, fairly empty 'frontier' areas and wilderness (used for resource extraction and tiny settlements like Indian reserves). This is important to understanding how Canada works.
